title: Why does `Integer a = 100; Integer b = 100; a == b` print `true` but `Integer a = 1000; Integer b = 1000; a == b` print `false` — autoboxing uses `Integer.valueOf`, which returns the SAME cached object for -128..127 but a NEW object outside that range (so `==` compares references), and why does `.equals()` always compare values — and how can the cache's upper bound be raised with `-Djava.lang.Integer.IntegerCache.high`?
shortTitle: Why Integer 100 == 100 is true but Integer 1000 == 1000 is false

s1_definition.profdef: When you write Integer a equals one hundred, the compiler autoboxes the literal by calling Integer.valueOf, and that method returns a shared cached instance for every value in the range minus one hundred twenty eight to one hundred twenty seven, so two Integers holding one hundred refer to the exact same object and the reference equality operator returns true. For one thousand, which is outside the cache, valueOf constructs a brand new Integer each time, so the two references point to different objects and the reference operator returns false, even though the numeric values are equal. The equals method, in contrast, is overridden in Integer to compare the underlying int values, so it always returns true when the values match regardless of object identity. The cache's upper bound defaults to one hundred twenty seven but can be raised at JVM startup with the system property java.lang.Integer.IntegerCache.high.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, imagine a tray of pre-printed, reusable tokens for small common amounts from minus one hundred twenty eight up to one hundred twenty seven. When two customers each ask for a token worth one hundred, the clerk hands out the very same pre-printed token both times, so holding the two tokens up side by side they are literally the one same token, and asking "is this the identical token" says yes. For one thousand there is no pre-printed token, so the clerk prints a fresh one each time, and now two tokens worth one thousand are two separate pieces of paper, so "is this the identical token" says no, even though both say one thousand. Asking instead "do these two tokens represent the same amount" always says yes when the amounts match, and that is what the equals method does. The bank can also ask the mint to pre-print a bigger range of tokens by setting a startup flag, which moves the boundary where the two questions start to disagree.
s1_definition.oneliner: valueOf hands back one shared cached object for minus one hundred twenty eight to one hundred twenty seven so `==` is true there, builds new objects outside that range so `==` is false, while equals always compares values, and the cache high bound is tunable with the IntegerCache.high flag.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When you write Integer a equals one hundred, the compiler autoboxes the literal by calling Integer.valueOf, and that method returns a shared cached instance for every value in the range minus one hundred twenty eight to one hundred twenty seven, so two Integers holding one hundred refer to the exact same object and the reference equality operator returns true. For one thousand, which is outside the cache, valueOf constructs a brand new Integer each time, so the two references point to different objects and the reference operator returns false, even though the numeric values are equal. The equals method, in contrast, is overridden in Integer to compare the underlying int values, so it always returns true when the values match regardless of object identity. The cache's upper bound defaults to one hundred twenty seven but can be raised at JVM startup with the system property java.lang.Integer.IntegerCache.high.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, imagine a tray of pre-printed, reusable tokens for small common amounts from minus one hundred twenty eight up to one hundred twenty seven. When two customers each ask for a token worth one hundred, the clerk hands out the very same pre-printed token both times, so holding the two tokens up side by side they are literally the one same token, and asking "is this the identical token" says yes. For one thousand there is no pre-printed token, so the clerk prints a fresh one each time, and now two tokens worth one thousand are two separate pieces of paper, so "is this the identical token" says no, even though both say one thousand. Asking instead "do these two tokens represent the same amount" always says yes when the amounts match, and that is what the equals method does. The bank can also ask the mint to pre-print a bigger range of tokens by setting a startup flag, which moves the boundary where the two questions start to disagree.

**One line to remember:** valueOf hands back one shared cached object for minus one hundred twenty eight to one hundred twenty seven so `==` is true there, builds new objects outside that range so `==` is false, while equals always compares values, and the cache high bound is tunable with the IntegerCache.high flag.

sections.s2_technical:
The behavior is entirely explained by how autoboxing is implemented. The statement `Integer a = 100;` does not call the Integer constructor; the compiler rewrites it to `Integer a = Integer.valueOf(100);`. The valueOf method checks whether the value falls within the cache, and if so it returns a reference to a pre-created Integer stored in a static array; otherwise it executes `new Integer(value)` and returns that fresh object. So for one hundred, both a and b receive the same cached reference, and `a == b`, which compares references, is true. For one thousand, both a and b receive freshly allocated objects, and `a == b` is false because the two references differ.

The reference equality operator on object types always compares identity, meaning whether the two references point to the same object in memory, never the contents. That is why it accidentally appears to work for small Integers, because identity happens to coincide with equality thanks to the cache, and then surprisingly fails for larger values where identity no longer coincides. Relying on this is a classic bug.

The equals method is the correct tool because Integer overrides Object's equals to compare the wrapped int values. So `a.equals(b)` returns true whenever the two Integers hold the same number, regardless of whether they are the same object or two distinct objects. For example `Integer big1 = 1000; Integer big2 = 1000; big1.equals(big2)` is true, and so is unboxing both to int and comparing with the operator, because then you are comparing primitive values directly.

The cache is a static nested class, IntegerCache, initialized when Integer is first loaded. It eagerly creates Integer objects for every value from minus one hundred twenty eight up to a high bound, defaulting to one hundred twenty seven. The high bound can be raised at startup with the flag `-Djava.lang.Integer.IntegerCache.high=1000`, which would make the earlier example print true for one thousand as well because one thousand would now be cached. The low bound is fixed at minus one hundred twenty eight and cannot be lowered.

Several senior points follow. First, this exact caching is mandated by the Java Language Specification for Integer, Short, Long, Byte, Character in the small ranges, and Boolean, so the minus one hundred twenty eight to one hundred twenty seven guarantee is portable, but anything relying on the high bound is not portable because it can be reconfigured. Second, Float and Double are never cached, so reference comparison on them is always unreliable. Third, because tuning the high bound changes behavior globally and invisibly, it is almost never done in practice except as a micro-optimization in memory-sensitive code, and it must never be used to make broken == comparisons appear to work. The firm rule for banking code is to compare wrapper values with equals or to unbox to primitives, and to treat any == between Integer objects as a defect unless both sides are known to be primitives.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A validation routine compared two Integer branch codes with the reference operator, and it passed all tests because the test data used small codes under one hundred twenty seven, then failed in production when a branch code of one thousand one was compared and the equal codes were treated as different. This is exactly the cache making == true inside the range and false outside.

Problem 2 — The team debated whether to just raise the cache high bound to make the comparison work, and the senior explained why that is the wrong fix. This is exactly the IntegerCache.high flag and its pitfalls.

Problem 3 — The correct fix replaced the reference comparison with equals, which compares values and works for every range. This is exactly why equals is the right tool.

The code contains a `CacheEqualityDemo` main class that compares branch codes inside and outside the cache with both == and equals, and prints what would change if the high bound were raised.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/core/CacheEqualityDemo.java

# Run with default cache (128 == 128 prints false)
java -cp out com.bank.core.CacheEqualityDemo

# Run with a raised cache high bound (now 1000 == 1000 would print true)
java -Djava.lang.Integer.IntegerCache.high=1000 -cp out com.bank.core.CacheEqualityDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two Integers holding one hundred, two holding one thousand, the boundary values one hundred twenty seven and one hundred twenty eight, and a read of the cache high property.

Step 1 — Assigning one hundred to smallA compiles to a call to Integer.valueOf, which finds one hundred inside the cache and returns the shared cached object. Assigning one hundred to smallB returns the identical cached object, so both references point to one object.

Step 2 — Comparing smallA and smallB with the reference operator compares identity, which is true because they are the same object. Comparing with equals compares values, which is also true.

Step 3 — Assigning one thousand to bigA calls valueOf, which finds one thousand outside the cache and constructs a new Integer. Assigning one thousand to bigB constructs another new Integer, so the two references point to different objects.

Step 4 — Comparing bigA and bigB with the reference operator is false because the identities differ, even though both hold one thousand. Comparing with equals is true because values match. Unboxing both to int and comparing with the operator is also true because primitives compare by value.

Step 5 — The boundary check shows one hundred twenty seven, the last cached value, comparing true, while one hundred twenty eight, the first uncached value, comparing false, pinpointing exactly where identity stops coinciding with equality.

Step 6 — The program reads the IntegerCache high system property. With the default run it reports the default, and the boundary behaves as above. If run with the flag raising the high bound to one thousand, one thousand would now be cached and its reference comparison would flip to true, demonstrating that the boundary is configurable and therefore unsafe to rely on.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The reason Integer one hundred compared with the reference operator prints true but Integer one thousand prints false comes entirely from how autoboxing is implemented. When I write Integer a equals one hundred, the compiler does not call the constructor; it rewrites this to Integer dot valueOf of one hundred. The valueOf method keeps a cache of pre-created Integer objects for every value from minus one hundred twenty eight to one hundred twenty seven, so for one hundred it returns the same shared cached object to both a and b. The reference operator compares object identity, and since both variables point to that one cached object, it reports true.

For one thousand, which is outside the cache, valueOf constructs a brand new Integer each time, so a and b point to two different objects. The reference operator now reports false, because it is comparing identity and the identities differ, even though both objects hold the numeric value one thousand. This is exactly why comparing wrapper objects with the reference operator is a bug: it accidentally works for small cached values and then silently fails for larger ones.

The correct tool is the equals method, which Integer overrides to compare the wrapped int values rather than object identity. So one thousand dot equals one thousand is always true because the values match, and so is unboxing both to primitive int and comparing them, because primitives compare by value. In our banking system this bit us when a branch code comparison using the reference operator passed every test with small codes but then treated two equal branch codes of one thousand one as different in production. The fix was to compare with equals, which is correct across every range.

The senior detail I always mention is the tunable boundary. The cache high bound defaults to one hundred twenty seven but can be raised at JVM startup with the system property for the Integer cache high value, so running with that flag set to one thousand would make one thousand cached and flip its reference comparison to true. The low bound of minus one hundred twenty eight is fixed and cannot be lowered. I stress that raising the bound is almost never the right fix, because it changes behavior globally and invisibly and makes non-portable code, and it must never be used to paper over a broken reference comparison. The portable, correct rule for banking code is simple: compare Integer values with equals or unbox to primitives, and treat any reference comparison between two Integer objects as a defect. I also note that Float and Double are never cached at all, so reference comparison on boxed floating values is always unreliable.
